# Llama-70B Episode Analysis Results

## Experiment: llama-70b-episodes
- **Model**: Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4
- **Environment**: ScienceWorld (11 task types × 20 episodes = 220 total)
- **Hypothesis**: DAF > 80% (death dominance scales to 70B)
- **Conclusion**: ✓ SUCCESS (DAF = 101.0%)

## Aggregate Metrics

| Metric | Value | 95% CI |
|--------|------:|--------|
| DAF | 101.0% | [95.3, 107.5] |
| delta_full (det − int) | 29.53 | [23.40, 35.87] |
| delta_nd (both-alive) | −0.30 | [−2.10, 1.38] |
| Label fraction | 91.3% | [84.1, 97.2] |
| Int death rate | 48.6% | [41.8, 55.0] |
| Det death rate | 20.0% | [15.0, 25.4] |
| Δ death rate | +28.6pp | [22.7, 34.5] |

## Label Distribution

| Label | Count | % |
|-------|------:|--:|
| det-preferred | 67 | 30.5% |
| internal-preferred | 2 | 0.9% |
| no-preference | 151 | 68.6% |

## Counterfactual Decomposition

| Category | Count |
|----------|------:|
| death_sole | 52 |
| death_and_score | 11 |
| non_death | 6 |
| no_preference | 151 |

## Per-Task Breakdown

| Task | Int DR | Det DR | delta_full | det-pref | int-pref |
|------|-------:|-------:|-----------:|---------:|---------:|
| chemistry-mix | 55.0% | 15.0% | 41.80 | 8 | 0 |
| find-animal | 55.0% | 20.0% | 35.40 | 7 | 0 |
| find-non-living-thing | 0.0% | 0.0% | −1.70 | 4 | 2 |
| freeze | 55.0% | 30.0% | 25.00 | 5 | 0 |
| grow-fruit | 50.0% | 35.0% | 15.00 | 3 | 0 |
| identify-life-stages-1 | 55.0% | 25.0% | 32.50 | 6 | 0 |
| identify-life-stages-2 | 50.0% | 25.0% | 25.00 | 5 | 0 |
| inclined-plane-determine-angle | 55.0% | 20.0% | 36.00 | 7 | 0 |
| lifespan-longest-lived | 50.0% | 25.0% | 27.50 | 5 | 0 |
| lifespan-longest-lived-then-shortest-lived | 55.0% | 15.0% | 43.30 | 8 | 0 |
| measure-melting-point-unknown-substance | 55.0% | 10.0% | 45.00 | 9 | 0 |

## Cross-Model Comparison

| Model | Size | DAF | delta_full | Int DR | Det DR |
|-------|------|----:|----------:|-------:|-------:|
| Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct | 7B | 90.4% | — | — | — |
| Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 8B | 88.2% | — | — | — |
| Gemma-2-9B-it | 9B | 89.7% | — | — | — |
| Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct-AWQ | 72B | 92.4% | — | — | — |
| **Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-AWQ** | **70B** | **101.0%** | **29.53** | **48.6%** | **20.0%** |

## Key Observations

1. **DAF=101.0% (>100%)**: Death-avoidance accounts for more than 100% of the deterministic agent's advantage, meaning when both agents survive, the internal agent actually performs slightly better (delta_nd=−0.30).

2. **Strongest death dominance across all models tested**: The 70B Llama shows the highest DAF and largest death rate gap (28.6pp) among all models.

3. **Near-perfect label fraction (91.3%)**: When there's a preference, 97.1% favor deterministic (67 vs 2), driven almost entirely by death avoidance.

4. **find-non-living-thing is the only zero-death task**: Both agents survive all episodes, and this is the only task showing slight internal-agent preference (2 episodes).

5. **Hypothesis confirmed**: DAF > 80% holds strongly. The death dominance pattern not only scales to 70B but intensifies.

## Bootstrap Details
- B = 10,000, seed = 42
- All 10,000 bootstrap samples produced valid DAF estimates
- DAF 95% CI lower bound (95.3%) still well above 80% threshold

36	\subsection{Multi-Model Validation (7--9B Tier)}
37	\label{sec:cross-model}
38	
39	A Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct~\citep{llama3-2024} cross-model replication across all 11 task types ($N{=}220$) confirms that death dominance replicates across model families: internal death rate $41.4\%$ vs.\ deterministic $11.4\%$ (death-rate differential $+30.0$~pp), DAF $= 88.2\%$ (95\% CI: $[80.2\%, 95.1\%]$; $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +33.17$, $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +3.9$), with direction consistency 10/10 on death-prone tasks, 83 deterministic-preferred, 3 internal-preferred (1.4\%, all death-asymmetry reversals), and 134 no-preference labels.
40	Both models show ${\sim}42\%$ internal vulnerability ($+26.5$ vs.\ $+30.0$~pp differential; per-task details in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}).
41	A third model family, Gemma-2-9B-it~\citep{gemma2-2024} (sliding window attention, vs.\ full attention in Qwen/Llama), independently confirms the pattern: DAF${=}89.7\%$ (95\% CI $[79.5\%, 98.4\%]$; $N{=}220$), with all 10 death-prone task types showing positive $\Delta$DR (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}). Three architecturally distinct models thus converge on DAF $88$--$90\%$ (spread 2.2~pp); $10{\times}$ scaling to 72B (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}) confirms persistence across capability levels (DAF${=}92.4\%$).

Category B dominates: agents demonstrate task comprehension but systematically fail to translate it into correct ScienceWorld actions. This taxonomy was produced by a single annotator; no inter-annotator agreement was computed. The categories are intended as qualitative illustrations, not as formal labels with reliability guarantees.

## Experiment: llama-70b-episodes
- **Model**: Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4

630	\section{Failure Mode Analysis}
631	\label{app:failure-modes}
632	
633	All 105 internal-strategy deaths (100\%) are triggered by the same action pattern: \texttt{focus on [object]}. In ScienceWorld, \texttt{focus on} is the answer-submission action (equivalent to ``this is my final answer''); the LLM agent systematically misuses it as a general interaction or exploration command, and applies it to irrelevant targets (rooms, doors, inventory items). Each such execution submits an incorrect answer and triggers the $-100$ death penalty. Within death episodes, both strategies exhibit comparable \texttt{focus on} rates (${\sim}5\%$); the internal strategy's higher death count (105 vs.\ 40 for deterministic) reflects how often each strategy enters catastrophic states, not different action selection within those states.
634	
635	Manual inspection identifies four failure categories: (A) no task awareness, where the agent executes \texttt{focus on} without reading the task; (B) task-aware but lacking action grounding, where the agent correctly identifies the objective but cannot map it to valid action primitives; (D) genuine attempts with execution failure; and (E) initial progress wasted by early errors. Category B dominates: agents demonstrate task comprehension but systematically fail to translate it into correct ScienceWorld actions. This taxonomy was produced by a single annotator; no inter-annotator agreement was computed. The categories are intended as qualitative illustrations, not as formal labels with reliability guarantees.
636	\label{tab:death-taxonomy}

639	\emph{Category A} (no task awareness): In a \texttt{chemistry-mix} episode, the agent immediately executes \texttt{focus on kitchen}, \texttt{focus on door}, \texttt{focus on inventory} without reading the task, dying on the first \texttt{focus on} call. \emph{Category B} (comprehension without grounding): In a \texttt{lifespan-longest-lived} episode, the agent correctly identifies that it must compare animal lifespans and reasons about which animal lives longest, but then executes \texttt{focus on oak tree} (a non-animal object in the room) instead of navigating to find the target animal, triggering death.

\paragraph{Oracle degeneracy and practical implications.}

Always-deterministic matches 96.3\% of oracle decisions (\S\ref{sec:baselines}), capping any router's marginal value at 2.89 points. $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = 2.84$ (9.6\% of total gap) shows the advantage concentrates almost entirely in death episodes; ALFWorld (DAF${=}0\%$) confirms the framework diagnoses qualitatively different mechanisms. A ${\sim}$50-episode pilot suffices for build-vs-buy decisions (Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}); action-space filtering reduces death rate by 19~pp (Appendix~\ref{app:grounding-ablation}). The decomposition applies when three conditions hold: binary catastrophic failures, asymmetric failure rates, and $P \gg \Delta_\text{nd}$---ScienceWorld satisfies all three; MATH and ALFWorld lack the first.

These approaches, which operate in non-catastrophic settings, share the assumption that routing signal stems from diverse sources and a learned router can exploit it---an assumption that remains untested: no prior work has systematically decomposed what drives routing preferences in interactive environments.

We propose a \emph{diagnostic framework} comprising (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), which decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding. This addresses a methodological gap: per-step oracle comparison degenerates under sparse rewards (97.4\% tie rate; \S\ref{sec:collection}), and keyword-based heuristics fail structurally (\S\ref{sec:baselines}). lines: \section*{Limitations}
\paragraph{Environmental scope.}

-Our primary analysis uses a single environment (ScienceWorld, 11 of 30 task types) with one backbone (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), though extended validation of representative excluded tasks confirms the pattern (Appendix~\ref{app:extended-validation}). The $-100$ death penalty amplifies DAF; environments with softer penalties would exhibit lower DAF values (Appendix~\ref{app:penalty}). The 19 excluded task types (63\%) lack routing signal because both strategies typically time out within 30 steps; increasing the step budget could surface non-death-dominated signal that our current setup does not capture. Cross-environment analyses on MATH and ALFWorld (\S\ref{sec:cross-env}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}) provide preliminary supporting evidence but do not conclusively establish generalization. A Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct cross-model replication (11 task types, $N{=}220$; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}) shows death dominance replicates with direction consistency 10/10 while vulnerability magnitude varies ($+30.0$~pp vs.\ Qwen $+26.5$~pp), though both models are in the 7--8B parameter range; Two 70B-class models (Qwen2.5-72B and Llama-3.1-70B; $10{\times}$ scale) reduce death rate but do not eliminate death dominance (DAF $92.4$--$101.0\%$; \S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}); validation beyond 70B remains future work. Whether death avoidance remains dominant for frontier models with substantially lower failure rates is an open question. Whether death avoidance remains dominant for frontier models with substantially lower failure rates is an open question. Our quantitative results (DAF $= 90.4\%$, label fractions) are specific to ScienceWorld; the framework's generality claim is methodological (the diagnostic procedure applies to any environment with asymmetric fatal outcomes), not empirical (the specific percentages may differ across environments).
\paragraph{Methodological constraints.}

Our internal-reasoning baseline uses single-pass ReAct~\citep{react-2023}. Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023} reduces death rate from 42.9\% to 31.4\% (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}), but more aggressive self-correction or Tree-of-Thought backtracking~\citep{tot-2023} may further reduce internal death rates. Episode-level labels assign a single routing preference to entire episodes, which may be suboptimal for individual steps (particularly those preceding death events). However, of 2{,}040 training steps only 0.3\% exhibit strict directional conflict (step-level oracle opposite to episode label); the remaining apparent mislabeling consists of episode labels applied to steps where neither strategy has a step-level advantage (60.3\% pre-event neutral). The issue is granularity mismatch (applying correct-direction labels to uninformative steps), not directional error. Training on pure-strategy trajectories also introduces distribution shift at deployment~\citep{dagger-2011}. Grounding ablation reduces but does not eliminate the death rate differential (from $+26.5$\,pp to approximately $+8$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:grounding-ablation}); Post-ablation counterfactual decomposition over matched episodes confirms that death remains the dominant signal source ({$\geq$}93\% of disambiguating labels arise from death asymmetry, with near-zero non-death performance gap $\Delta_\text{nd} \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:grounding-ablation}). Under mixed-strategy routing with oracle death prediction, switching to deterministic at the step before death could reduce the internal death rate; even under optimistic assumptions (perfect step-level death prediction), a residual gap of ${>}10$~pp between strategies is expected, as fatal trajectories involve cumulative hallucination errors preceding the death event. More broadly, projecting episode-level labels onto 10--50 sequential steps with path-dependent state introduces compounding error: early routing decisions alter the state trajectory, potentially invalidating later labels derived from the episode outcome.

lines: We test whether agent-level improvement reduces death dominance (Table~\ref{tab:agent-improvement}). Retry ($N{=}5$ attempts without self-correction) yields marginal reduction on death-prone tasks ($43.5\%$ vs.\ $48.0\%$ baseline, $\Delta = -4.5$~pp). Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023}\footnote{Reflexion uses a fixed allocation of 20 episodes per task type ($20 \times 11 = 220$), vs.\ the baseline's variable 20--40 per type ($N{=}245$).} (verbal self-reflection between trials) reduces death to 31.4\% across all 11 tasks by rescuing 29.3\% of first-trial deaths, but the gap to deterministic remains 15.1~pp; on the 10 death-prone tasks, Reflexion achieves ${\sim}$35\%. Under Reflexion ($N{=}3$, matched-episode analysis), $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = -0.47$, yielding DAF $> 100\%$: the deterministic advantage is entirely attributable to death avoidance, and in non-death episodes the self-correcting agent slightly outperforms the deterministic baseline. Scaling to Qwen2.5-72B ($10{\times}$ parameters; both strategies independently collected at 72B, 255 episodes across all 11 task types) reduces death rate to $30.6\%$. The 72B deterministic strategy achieves $2.75\%$ death rate ($\Delta\text{DR} = +27.8$~pp), and $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.28$, yielding DAF $= 92.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[86.1\%, 97.9\%]$; 7B: $90.4\%$), with 5 internal-preferred episodes (vs.\ 9 at 7B; $2.0\%$ vs.\ $3.7\%$).

A second 70B-class model, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct ($N{=}220$), intensifies the pattern: internal death rate $48.6\%$, deterministic $20.0\%$ ($\Delta\text{DR} = +28.6$~pp), $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = -0.30$, yielding DAF $= 101.0\%$ (95\% CI: $[95.3\%, 107.5\%]$). DAF exceeding 100\% indicates that death avoidance more than fully explains the deterministic advantage---when both agents survive, the internal agent performs comparably or slightly better. Label fraction rises to $91.3\%$ (67 det-preferred, 2 int-preferred; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}).

-Two independent 70B-class models thus confirm that $10{\times}$ scaling does not attenuate death dominance; it intensifies proportional dominance because the deterministic strategy's safety gains outpace the internal strategy's ($2.75$--$20.0\%$ vs.\ $30.6$--$48.6\%$).

+Two independent 70B-class models thus confirm that $10{\times}$ scaling does not attenuate death dominance; it intensifies proportional dominance because the deterministic strategy maintains substantially lower death rates than the internal strategy at both 70B scales ($2.75$--$20.0\%$ vs.\ $30.6$--$48.6\%$).
\paragraph{Dose-response analysis.}

We extend both interventions to $N{=}5$ trials on death-prone tasks ($n{=}200$; Figure~\ref{fig:dose-response}). Retry is nearly flat ($48.0\% \to 43.5\%$). Reflexion drops steeply to $34.0\%$ at $N{=}3$ ($\Delta = -13.5$~pp, $p = 0.003$) then stabilizes ($34$--$36.5\%$ for $N \geq 3$, pairwise $p > 0.5$); both the decline and plateau are well-powered (MDE ${\sim}8$~pp at 80\% power; Appendix~\ref{app:dose-response}).
